title: Delivery Radius Checker: See Your Zone
description: Set your hub, set a delivery radius, and see which areas fall inside with the Delivery Radius Checker — before you promise coverage. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, a 5-mile ring around a depot includes the suburb at 4.6 miles and excludes the one at 5.4 — the checker turns 'we probably cover that' into a visible line.
quick_answer: The Delivery Radius Checker draws your delivery radius around your hub on a live map so you can see which areas fall inside the service zone. Locate the depot, set the distance, and review the coverage against the neighbourhoods and postcodes you serve — before a customer tests it.

faq: Drive time or radius — which should I publish?
Radius is simpler to explain; drive time is honester to experience. Many businesses draw the radius here for the promise, then sanity-check its far corners by road and trim exceptions manually.
Is a radius the same as driving distance?
No — the ring is straight-line geometry. A 5-mile ring contains places 8 road-miles away. The checker shows the promise; routing tools price the journey.
Can I use this for service-area planning?
Yes — it is the visual first pass of service planning. Follow it with population counts and road checks before the zone becomes a public promise.
Are map measurements legal survey measurements?
No, and they do not need to be: a delivery zone is a business policy drawn at map accuracy, not a legal boundary.
What if my zone should follow roads or a river?
Then a circle is the wrong shape — draw the real boundary as a polygon with the drawn-area tools and list the towns inside it.
Can I check a customer's address precisely?
Set the hub, set the radius, and read the map at the address — inside or outside is visible. For a numeric answer, measure hub-to-address directly.
Miles or kilometres?
Both are supported; US operations usually publish miles, European ones kilometres. The ring does not care which the policy is written in.
Can I check more than one depot?
Draw each depot's ring in turn and compare where they overlap — the overlap is double-covered ground your rota can exploit or your zones should partition.
The ring includes an area we would never serve. Now what?
That is the checker doing its job: either trim the radius, carve a polygon zone instead, or publish the exception. All three beat discovering it via a complaint.
Does it work for collection rounds as well?
Yes — any 'within X of base' promise draws the same ring: collections, callouts, service engineer patches.
